brief: Maths Standard bivariate data and probability (root request, 19 November 2026), methods of brief 243
purpose: Research route inputs for Claude, not a canonical route or teaching approval
syllabus: Mathematics Standard 11-12 (2024), Year 12 Standard 2 and Standard 1
identifierPolicy: Exact CMS codenames; official sourceHtml preserves mathematical layout. Year 12 entries list Standard 2 and Standard 1 codenames separately (standard2ActionIds, standard1ActionIds); syllabusActions carries both, each with its course.

officialEvidence.source: NSW Curriculum Year 12 Standard 2 and Standard 1 Bivariate data analysis and Relative frequency and probability pages, as recorded in the crosswalk (read 18 November 2026)

siteSource.note: Paths are repo paths at this commit, read from the read-only local clone C:/Users/kygs/teaching-app-fix at the same commit (not modified). SHA256 values recomputed from the clone on 19 November 2026 and match the crosswalk inventory. Bivariate data analysis lessons 04 to 11 (numbered L01 to L08 on the page, MS-69) and Relative frequency and probability lessons 01 to 04 use data-step-id sections and label worked examples we-1 to we-3 (bivariate lesson11 has we-1 only).

recommendations: Run b01 to b07 then p01 to p08 after Trigonometry (root rulings 28 and 46: playlist positions 62 to 76, as the outline table). Standard 2 students take all fifteen. Standard 1 students take b01 to b04, b07, p01 to p03, p05, p06 and p08 (ten videos); b05, b06, p04 and p07 are Standard 2 only. Split parts, if root accepts them, share their number.

Joins: b01 opens on t11's final frame (ruling 64) and confirms the beach kiosk board as its opening picture (ruling 59 closed by this pack): headings 'top temperature (°C)' and 'ice creams sold', five rows filled in b01 with the site's own lesson08 activity data (18, 22, 25, 28, 32°C; 40, 60, 75, 90, 120 ice creams), so one dataset carries b01 to b07. t05's Standard 1 panel is the same board. b07 ends on the kiosk board with tomorrow's forecast ('20% chance of rain'), which opens p01. p08 ends two ways: Standard 2 to math-s12-z01 (its pack's bakery loaves, accepted here), Standard 1 to the end of Year 12 content.

Two-route final frames (ruling 38 pattern): b04 (Standard 2 to b05, Standard 1 to b07), p03 (Standard 2 to p04, Standard 1 to p05), p06 (Standard 2 to p07, Standard 1 to p08) and p08 (Standard 2 to z01, Standard 1 done). Where a Standard 2 video rejoins the Standard 1 path (b06 to b07, p04 to p05, p07 to p08), its final frame repeats the Standard 1 panel exactly, so the next video has one opening.

Outline problem (entry knowledge): the brief asks for Year 11 Standard data and probability points, but the 2024 Year 11 Standard course has no probability focus area. p01 assumes Stage 4 and 5 chance only (as t01 did for trigonometry). The outline's dependency list (b01: cic8a0b6e9; b04: ci94641a48, cic0a28004, ci4777471a) is right; b07 also builds on ci4777471a and ci1b3cf962 (math-s11-l04), which the list attaches only to b04.

Notation (decision for Claude): the site writes the line as y = mx + b (lesson08) and y = a + bx (lesson09) and says 'the HSC uses y = a + bx'; the 2024 bivariate points name no form, and Year 11 teaches y = mx + c (ciafd3b572). Suggested: y = mx + c on screen throughout, with the calculator's A + Bx read as 'A is the intercept, B is the gradient' (MS-63).

Pace flags (gentler Standard pace): b04 at risk (suggested split b04a, both courses, and b04b, Standard 2 only); b02, b06, p03, p04, p07 and p08 to watch; b01, b03, b05, b07, p01, p02 and p05 fit 6 to 9 minutes; p06 is short (no padding).

Advanced reuse (ruling 7): the Year 11 Advanced probability kit (OutcomeArray, ProbabilityTree, VennDiagram, TwoWayTable in a11-prob-parts.tsx; RollSimulator, ProbabilityBars, SpinnerSectors and OutcomeGrid in prob-parts.tsx; RunningMeanTrace in spread-parts.tsx; seededRandom and tallyOf in stat-math.ts) covers the probability strand. Advanced anchors are not reused (water polo caps, two-scoop ice cream cones, a library, a gumball machine, a hotel's rooms, traffic lights, a food delivery app, two alarms, mandarins, a homemade spinner, a theme-park ride, a board-game die rolled 200 times, a tear-off calendar, pet insurance, sprinters, a parcel tracker, a cookie, a bus every ten minutes, a running playlist, chip bags, apples, fishing catches, a bottle filler). No Advanced video teaches scatter plots, correlation or regression, so the bivariate strand needs a new ScatterBoard.

No gambling (ruling 6): probability uses neutral objects (marbles, coins, dice, spinners, counters) and everyday events (forecasts, rideshares, canteen choices, sport shots). The site's raffle (lesson03 SA 2) and 52-card deck (lesson01 we-2) are left out. All new data in the packs are invented and labelled as such; no real dataset is quoted without a dated source.

Site findings: MS-60 to MS-69 appended to docs/production/claude-pm/site-corrections-maths-standard.md, section 10 (three strength scales for r, a categorical variable given an r, a missing one-variable contrast and non-linear form, mixed line notation with b meaning two things, a pause card contradicting the beyond-syllabus notice, an impossible baby-height model, an electricity model that runs the wrong way for summer, a muddled causal checklist and drowning contexts, P(B|A) notation, gambling and medical contexts, and mismatched lesson numbering and unsourced hooks). Every site worked value was recalculated and matches.

Kit needs for both strands are in docs/production/claude-pm/checks/maths-standard-kit-needs-b-p.md; the main new part is a ScatterBoard (table rows lifting into points, form, direction and strength cues, a line by eye with an above-and-below counter, the mean point, a digital trendline, an r dial, interpolation and extrapolation zones), with a STAT-mode option on StudioToolPanel and a ChanceLine and ClaimCard for the probability strand.
covers: math-s12-b01 to math-s12-b07 (Year 12 Bivariate data analysis) and math-s12-p01 to math-s12-p08 (Year 12 Relative frequency and probability), Standard 2 and Standard 1

entries.stopBoundary: Pearson's correlation coefficient r: between −1 and 1; its sign gives the direction and its size the strength of a linear association; r = 1, −1 and 0 as pictures; one strength guide used consistently (|r| from 0.8 strong, 0.5 to 0.8 moderate, below 0.5 weak, as a guide, not a rule); r from a scientific calculator in two-variable STAT mode (enter the pairs, read r), reported to two decimal places; two checks (r stays between −1 and 1; its sign matches the plot); limits: r measures straight-line association only (a curve can have a high r or an r near 0), one outlier can move it a lot, and a large r does not show cause. Stops before the least-squares line (b06).

entries.stopBoundary: P(event) = number of favourable outcomes ÷ total number of outcomes, only when the outcomes are equally likely (the ten marbles are; the three colours are not); simplify and convert; the complement: P(not E) = 1 − P(E), and when it is quicker than counting; an impossible event (a green marble, 0) and a certain one. Stops before two-stage events (p03).
entries.recommendation: Keep the site's marbles (P(blue) = 1/2, P(not blue) = 1/2, P(green) = 0), die (P(even) = 1/2, P(not a 6) = 5/6), class of 30 (12 study French: 2/5 = 0.4 = 40%, complement 3/5), box of 15 balls (7/15, 11/15) and STATISTICS (3/10). The 52-card deck (site we-2) is left out (neutral objects, ruling 6). Pace: fits.

entries.mainLearnerQuestion: How do arrays and tree diagrams list the outcomes of a two-stage event?

syllabusActions.text: Construct and use arrays, tree diagrams and probability trees to determine the outcomes and probabilities for multistage events
syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Construct and use arrays, tree diagrams and probability trees to determine the outcomes and probabilities for multistage events

syllabusActions.text: Represent equally likely outcomes using arrays and tree diagrams to solve problems, involving replacement where applicable, in two-stage events
syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Represent equally likely outcomes using arrays and tree diagrams to solve problems, involving replacement where applicable, in two-stage events

entryKnowledge.text: ci6224eb8c, ci566abb19 (S1: ci7cb75229, ciefced297): favourable ÷ total, the complement.

entries.startBoundary: p02's final frame (proposed): a school canteen's lunch-deal board, 3 mains and 4 drinks, one of each picked at random: 'how many different lunches?'.
entries.stopBoundary: A two-stage event; an array (one stage across, the other down; every cell one outcome) and a tree diagram (one branch per outcome at each stage; every path one outcome), with replacement (the second draw starts from the full bag); probabilities by counting equally likely cells or paths; the multiplication principle for the total. Standard 1 stops here (two-stage, equally likely). Standard 2's branch probabilities and multiplying along a path are p04. Two-route final frame: Standard 2 to p04, Standard 1 to p05.
entries.recommendation: Keep the site's die and coin array (n(S) = 12, P(head and even) = 3/12 = 1/4, P(tail or less than 3) = 8/12 = 2/3) and the bag of 3 blue and 2 red with replacement, drawn as five lettered marbles so all 25 ordered pairs are equally likely (BB 9/25, at least one blue 21/25). Shares cice3fd0ea with p04. Pace: watch.

entries.mainLearnerQuestion: How do probability trees and P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B) handle multistage events?

syllabusActions.siteGap: Covered; lesson02 also writes P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B|A), conditional notation the Standard syllabus does not use (MS-66).

entryKnowledge.text: cice3fd0ea: arrays and tree diagrams for two-stage events.

entries.startBoundary: p03's Standard 2 panel (proposed): the 3 blue, 2 red tree from p03 with its four paths, the branch labels replaced by '?': 'can we write a probability on each branch?'.
entries.stopBoundary: A probability tree: a probability on each branch, the branches from one point add to 1; multiply along a path for one outcome, P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B); add the paths that make an event; all the paths add to 1 (the check); without replacement, the second-stage branches change because the bag has changed; three stages (three coins, 8 paths); unequal everyday chances (a bus and a train each on time). Ends on a frame shared with p03's Standard 1 panel.
entries.recommendation: Standard 2 only. Keep the site's with-replacement tree (9/25, 6/25, 6/25, 4/25; same colour 13/25; at least one blue 21/25) and without-replacement tree (2 red, 3 blue: 1/10, 3/10, 3/10, 3/10; one of each 3/5). Describe the changed branches in words, not with P(B|A) (MS-66). Pace: watch.

entryKnowledge.text: ci6224eb8c (S1: ci7cb75229): theoretical probability from equally likely outcomes.
cia7a007a6: frequency tables (a tally of results).

entries.startBoundary: One frame shared by p04's final frame and p03's Standard 1 panel (proposed): a coin and a tally card '10 flips: 7 heads': 'is this coin unfair?'.
entries.stopBoundary: Relative frequency = number of times the event happened ÷ number of trials, as an estimate of a probability, especially when no theoretical probability exists (how often a rideshare arrives within 5 minutes); more trials give relative frequencies that settle closer to the theoretical probability (a running proportion drawn live), but no finite run is guaranteed and the next flip is not 'due'; comparing an estimate with a theoretical value. Stops before expected frequency (p06).
entries.recommendation: Keep the site's coin (7/10 = 0.7 against 5037/10 000 = 0.5037), the die rolled 120 times (22, 18, 24, 19, 21, 16; all within 0.034 of 1/6) and the spinner (28/80 = 0.35 against 0.30). A live simulation shows the settling. Pace: fits.

entries.startBoundary: p05's final frame (proposed): the rideshare app's record '40 of the last 50 rides arrived within 5 minutes' and a calendar of 30 upcoming trips: 'how many on time?'.
entries.stopBoundary: Expected frequency = np (n trials, probability p each time), with p from theory or from a relative frequency; the answer is a long-run average, not a promise, and can be a decimal; using it to plan (stock, staff, spares). Two-route final frame: Standard 2 to p07, Standard 1 to p08.
entries.recommendation: Keep the site's 120 rolls → 20 sixes, 100 rolls → about 16.7, 2% of 500 bulbs → 10 and the factory's 15 faults in 500 → 60 expected in 2000. The site's raffle (SA 2), drug trial (SA 3) and genetic marker (we-2) are left out (owner note MS-68). Pace: fits, short; no padding (ruling 52 pattern).

syllabusActions.sourceHtml: Construct and interpret Venn diagrams and two-way tables from given information, limited to combinations of two attributes, and use them to solve problems in a variety of contexts

entryKnowledge.text: ci6224eb8c, ci566abb19: favourable ÷ total, and the complement for 'neither'.
cic1f6796f: categorical data in tables.

entries.startBoundary: p06's Standard 2 panel (proposed): a canteen survey card, 'bought lunch?' and 'bought recess?', with some students ticking both: 'how do we count the overlap once?'.
entries.stopBoundary: Two attributes; a Venn diagram (two overlapping circles in a rectangle; fill the overlap first, then each 'only' region, then 'neither'); a two-way table (four cells, row and column totals, a grand total; missing values by subtraction); moving between the two; probabilities from a region or cell ÷ the total; 'of those who...' fractions read from one row or column; 'at least one', 'exactly one' and 'neither' in words. Ends on a frame shared with p06's Standard 1 panel.
entries.recommendation: Standard 2 only. Keep the site's class of 30 (12 sport, 10 music, 5 both: 7, 5, 5, 13; at least one 17/30), the cohort of 120 (52, 20, 28, 20; 13/30, 5/6, 1/6) and the 150-person exercise and diet table (8/15, 55/80 = 11/16, 1/3). Advanced a11-s02 (two-scoop cones), s03 (library) and s05 (hotel rooms) anchors are not reused. Pace: watch.

entries.startBoundary: One frame shared by p07's final frame and p06's Standard 1 panel (proposed): a phone showing an invented app advertisement, '4 out of 5 users sleep better!', with a small grey footnote '25 volunteers': 'should we believe it?'.
entries.stopBoundary: How media, governments and companies use statistics and probabilities to make and sell decisions; five questions for any claim (how many were asked, how they were chosen, a percentage of what, relative or absolute change, who ran or paid for it); relative against absolute risk (2% to 1% is 'halved' but one percentage point); a survey percentage as a relative frequency from a sample; companies planning with expected frequency (warranties, spares, staffing); a government decision from data (invented, labelled). Two-route final frame (accepting the z01 pack's proposal): left, 'Standard 2: next, the normal distribution', a bakery's quality sheet with 200 loaves labelled 700 g weighed, the masses dropping into a coded histogram, 'what shape is this?'; right, a grey chip 'Standard 1: Year 12 course complete' pointing to the Year 12 Standard playlist.
